chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: After Strayhorn's death and learning from everyone
summary: He says Strayhorn left unfinished work, repeats the compiler idea, and says one can learn from any musician.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: When Strayhorn died, did this affect Duke's writing by not having Strayhorn to depend on?

Well, there were so many things left unfinished that Strayhorn did, till many of the things that you think were new, were things that Strayhorn left unfinished. And course they're a lot of tunes that you think weren't written by him, but they were, really. Basically. Because that's what the band -- we did mostly. You take a piece from him, this one and that one, and put them together. There again the compiler influence, not the composer, the compiler. And that was any amount of that that went on.
Do you think Duke learned a lot from Billy Strayhorn?

Oh, I think everyone of us learned a lot from everybody else. Yeah, in fact, I am of the opinion that there is no man that you can't learn something from. I mean musically and otherwise. Any musician you know, take our instruments we'll say, take mine, a trombone, there's something that some man -- any man can play that you haven't thought of playing, a little quirk, a little slide a little this or that. So you can learn something from everybody. See.
